questions.question: How do you run a Spring Boot application using Maven?
questions.title: Running Spring Boot with Maven: mvn spring-boot:run
questions.direct_answer: 'mvn spring-boot:run' starts your Spring Boot application directly through Maven using the spring-boot-maven-plugin — it compiles the code and starts the embedded server without creating a JAR first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Spring Boot development workflow knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the difference between 'mvn spring-boot:run' and 'java -jar' — one is for development, the other for production
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that 'mvn spring-boot:run' uses the exploded classpath (not a fat JAR) which is useful for hot reload with DevTools

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: During development, 'mvn spring-boot:run' is the most convenient way to start your Spring Boot application. This command is provided by the spring-boot-maven-plugin that you get automatically from spring-boot-starter-parent. It compiles your code and then starts the embedded Tomcat server — no need to package a JAR first. It runs with the expanded classpath, meaning each class and resource file is loaded directly rather than from a JAR, which supports faster hot reload. If you have spring-boot-devtools on your classpath, changes to class files trigger an automatic restart without you having to manually stop and restart. Under the hood, this command is different from running the packaged JAR — it uses the Maven build classpath rather than a fat JAR, which makes it faster to iterate. For production or any non-development deployment, you'd always use 'mvn package' followed by 'java -jar target/app.jar' — the packaged executable JAR. 'mvn spring-boot:run' is purely a development convenience.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'mvn spring-boot:run': development convenience — compiles and starts embedded server without creating JAR
Provided by spring-boot-maven-plugin (from spring-boot-starter-parent)
Runs with expanded classpath — supports hot reload with Spring Boot DevTools
Development only — not used for production deployments
Production: 'mvn package' → 'java -jar target/your-app.jar'

sections.hook: You want to run your Spring Boot app locally without packaging a JAR first. One Maven command does exactly that.

beats.content: mvn spring-boot:run compiles your code and starts the embedded Tomcat in one step. No target JAR required. It's provided by the spring-boot-maven-plugin, which you get automatically from spring-boot-starter-parent.

It uses an expanded classpath — class files and resources load directly from disk rather than from a packaged JAR. That's what makes hot reload work. When you add spring-boot-devtools, a file change triggers an automatic Spring context restart in one to three seconds.

candidates miss: mvn spring-boot:run is development-only. Never use it in a production Dockerfile or CI deployment step. The proper production flow is mvn clean package to build the fat JAR, then java -jar to run it.

sections.cap: mvn spring-boot:run is a developer shortcut. Fast to start, supports hot reload, no packaging required. Switch to java -jar for anything that goes beyond your local machine.

questions.question: What does the spring-boot-maven-plugin do and why is it essential for Spring Boot projects?
questions.title: spring-boot-maven-plugin
questions.direct_answer: The spring-boot-maven-plugin repackages the compiled JAR into an executable fat JAR containing all dependencies and an embedded server — without it, 'mvn package' produces a thin JAR that cannot run standalone.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring Boot's executable JAR is created and what makes it 'executable'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that removing the spring-boot-maven-plugin would produce a non-executable JAR — a common debugging scenario
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the BOOT-INF structure of the fat JAR and Spring's custom class loader for the nested JARs

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The spring-boot-maven-plugin is what transforms a standard Maven build into something that produces a self-contained, executable Spring Boot application. Without it, 'mvn package' produces a thin JAR containing only your application's compiled classes — it has no dependencies bundled in, so running 'java -jar' would fail immediately with a ClassNotFoundException for Spring, Jackson, or anything else. What the plugin does is bind to the 'package' phase and run a 'repackage' goal. It takes the thin JAR that Maven already built and repackages it into a fat JAR — also called an executable JAR or über-JAR. This fat JAR contains your application's classes in BOOT-INF/classes/, all dependency JARs nested inside BOOT-INF/lib/, and a special Spring Boot class loader (JarLauncher) that knows how to load classes from these nested JARs. The MANIFEST.MF points to the JarLauncher as the Main-Class. When you run 'java -jar app.jar', Java starts the JarLauncher, which sets up the classpath from the nested JARs and then starts your actual @SpringBootApplication. It also provides the 'spring-boot:run' goal for development.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Repackages thin JAR → fat/executable JAR containing all dependencies and embedded server
Fat JAR structure: BOOT-INF/classes (your code), BOOT-INF/lib (all dependency JARs)
Uses JarLauncher as Main-Class to load classes from nested JARs
Without this plugin: 'mvn package' produces a thin JAR that won't run standalone
Also provides 'spring-boot:run' goal for development and 'spring-boot:build-image' for OCI images

sections.hook: Without one specific plugin, mvn package builds a JAR that immediately crashes when you try to run it. That plugin is spring-boot-maven-plugin.

beats.content: Maven's default JAR packaging produces a thin JAR — only your compiled classes, no dependencies included. Running java -jar on it throws ClassNotFoundException for Spring itself, because Spring's JARs aren't in there.

The spring-boot-maven-plugin fixes this by binding a repackage goal to the package phase. After Maven creates the thin JAR, the plugin repackages it into a fat JAR that contains everything: your classes, all dependency JARs, and an embedded Tomcat.

beats.label: Inside the fat JAR:
items: BOOT-INF/classes/ — your compiled application classes
BOOT-INF/lib/ — all dependency JARs nested inside
MANIFEST.MF — points to JarLauncher as Main-Class
JarLauncher — Spring's custom class loader for loading nested JARs

beats.content: non-obvious: the plugin preserves the original thin JAR as app.jar.original. That lets library authors inspect what their artifact looks like before repackaging. It also means you can check what the thin JAR contains when debugging.

sections.cap: spring-boot-maven-plugin is what makes the fat JAR possible. It's the bridge between a standard Maven build and a self-contained deployable Spring Boot application.

questions.question: What is the workflow to package and run a Spring Boot application using Maven?
questions.title: Package and Run Spring Boot: mvn package + java -jar
questions.direct_answer: Run 'mvn clean package' to build the executable fat JAR in the target/ directory, then run 'java -jar target/your-app-version.jar' to start the application — no server installation required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic production deployment knowledge — how do you actually run a Spring Boot app?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the JAR filename includes the version from pom.xml — ls target/ to find the exact name
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention passing JVM arguments and Spring properties via command line: 'java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar --server.port=8081'

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The two-step workflow is: first build the JAR, then run it. Step one: 'mvn clean package'. The 'clean' removes any previous build output, and 'package' runs the full default lifecycle — compile, test, package — producing an executable fat JAR in the target/ directory. The JAR name follows the pattern artifactId-version.jar from your pom.xml, so it might be my-service-1.0.0.jar. Step two: 'java -jar target/my-service-1.0.0.jar'. Java finds the Main-Class in the JAR manifest, Spring's JarLauncher starts, and your Spring Boot application begins. You can pass JVM arguments before -jar: 'java -Xmx512m -Xms256m -jar app.jar'. You can also override Spring Boot properties after the JAR filename: 'java -jar app.jar --server.port=8081 --spring.profiles.active=prod'. This is handy for running multiple instances with different ports or environments. In production, you'd typically wrap this in a systemd service file, a Docker container, or let Kubernetes manage the lifecycle.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Step 1: 'mvn clean package' — produces target/artifactId-version.jar
Step 2: 'java -jar target/your-app.jar' — starts the application
JAR filename: {artifactId}-{version}.jar from pom.xml coordinates
JVM args: 'java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar'
Spring properties override: 'java -jar app.jar --server.port=8081 --spring.profiles.active=prod'

sections.hook: Two commands. That's all it takes to go from source code to a running Spring Boot application. No server installation, no deployment config.

beats.label: The two-step workflow:
items: mvn clean package: cleans old output, then compiles, tests, and packages into a fat JAR
java -jar target/your-app-1.0.0.jar: starts the embedded server and launches the app

beats.content: The JAR filename follows the pattern artifactId-version.jar from pom.xml. If you're not sure of the exact name, check the target/ directory. The fat JAR will typically be 30-80 MB because it bundles all dependencies.

beats.label: Useful runtime options:
items: JVM heap: java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar
Different port: java -jar app.jar --server.port=8081
Spring profile: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
Both: java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar --server.port=8081 --spring.profiles.active=prod

beats.content: non-obvious: Spring Boot properties passed as command-line arguments (--key=value) override everything else in the property resolution hierarchy — they beat application.properties, environment variables, and profile-specific files.

sections.cap: Build with mvn clean package, run with java -jar. In production, wrap that java -jar command in a Dockerfile or systemd service. The pattern stays the same.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot DevTools and how does it enable hot reload?
questions.title: Spring Boot DevTools and Hot Reload
questions.direct_answer: spring-boot-devtools is a development dependency that monitors classpath changes and triggers an automatic application restart when you recompile — significantly speeding up development iteration compared to full manual restarts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Developer experience and productivity awareness — DevTools is a common first-day setup question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that DevTools is automatically excluded from production JARs because it's test/runtime scoped
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the two-ClassLoader trick DevTools uses — it keeps a base ClassLoader and restarts only the application ClassLoader for faster restarts vs full JVM restarts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot DevTools is a development-time dependency that dramatically speeds up the code-change-see-result cycle. Without it, every change to your code requires you to manually stop the running app, rebuild, and restart — which can take 10-30 seconds. With DevTools added to your pom.xml (in test scope typically), it watches the classpath for changes. When you recompile a class in your IDE, DevTools detects the .class file change and automatically restarts the Spring application context. The restart is much faster than a full restart because DevTools uses two ClassLoaders: a 'base' ClassLoader that loads your dependencies (which rarely change) and a 'restart' ClassLoader that loads your application classes. When a restart is triggered, only the restart ClassLoader is recreated — the base dependencies stay loaded. This typically cuts restart time to 1-3 seconds instead of 10-20. DevTools also disables template caching so Thymeleaf/Freemarker changes show immediately. Importantly, the spring-boot-maven-plugin automatically excludes DevTools from the production fat JAR — it's a development-only dependency and should not run in production.

sections.title: Key Points
content: DevTools monitors classpath changes and triggers automatic Spring context restart
Two ClassLoader trick: base (dependencies) stays loaded, only app ClassLoader restarts — faster
Typical restart time: 1-3 seconds vs 10-30 seconds for full app restart
Also disables template caching for immediate HTML template changes
Automatically excluded from production fat JAR by spring-boot-maven-plugin

sections.hook: Without DevTools, every code change means a manual stop-rebuild-restart cycle. With it, your app restarts automatically in one to three seconds.

beats.content: Add spring-boot-devtools to pom.xml (in test scope). Now when you recompile a class in IntelliJ, DevTools detects the .class file change on disk and automatically restarts the Spring application context. No manual stop-restart needed.

The speed secret is two ClassLoaders. The base ClassLoader loads your dependencies, which rarely change. The restart ClassLoader loads your application classes. On restart, only the restart ClassLoader is recreated — dependencies stay loaded. That's why it's 1-3 seconds instead of 10-20.

beats.label: Other DevTools features:
items: Disables Thymeleaf and Freemarker template caching — HTML changes show immediately
Enables H2 console by default in dev
LiveReload browser extension integration for automatic browser refresh

beats.content: gotcha: DevTools auto-detects that it's running in a fat JAR and disables itself. The spring-boot-maven-plugin also excludes it from the packaged JAR. It's designed to never reach production accidentally.

sections.cap: DevTools is a first-day-of-development setup item. Add it, let your IDE auto-compile on save, and your feedback loop drops from 20 seconds to 2. It stays out of production automatically.

questions.question: When would you package a Spring Boot application as a WAR instead of a JAR?
questions.title: WAR Packaging in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Package as WAR when deploying to a traditional external servlet container (Tomcat, JBoss, WebSphere) that manages multiple applications — though modern deployments strongly prefer the self-contained executable JAR approach.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of different deployment models — enterprise companies often have requirements for WAR deployment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking WAR deployment is legacy and never needed — many enterprise companies with existing app server infrastructure still require it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a Spring Boot WAR can also be run as an executable JAR — Spring Boot is clever enough to support both modes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The modern Spring Boot default is to package as an executable JAR with an embedded Tomcat server. This is the self-contained, 'just run java -jar' approach and is ideal for containers, cloud, and microservices. However, some enterprise environments — banks, large corporations, government systems — have existing application server infrastructure like Tomcat, JBoss, WebSphere, or WebLogic running in their data centers. These organizations may have policies requiring all web applications to be deployed as WARs to their managed app server, rather than running standalone JARs. To produce a WAR from Spring Boot: change packaging to 'war' in pom.xml, mark spring-boot-starter-tomcat as 'provided' scope (since the external Tomcat provides the servlet container), and have your main class extend SpringBootServletInitializer. Interestingly, Spring Boot WAR packaging is smart — the same WAR can be deployed to an external Tomcat AND run as 'java -jar app.war'. It supports both modes, which is handy during the migration period.

sections.title: Key Points
content: JAR (default): self-contained, embedded Tomcat, 'java -jar' — ideal for cloud/containers
WAR: for deploying to external servlet containers (Tomcat, JBoss, WebSphere)
WAR setup: packaging=war, spring-boot-starter-tomcat scope=provided, extend SpringBootServletInitializer
Spring Boot WARs are dual-mode: can run as 'java -jar' OR deploy to external Tomcat
Modern recommendation: prefer JAR unless enterprise infrastructure requires WAR

sections.hook: JAR is the modern default. WAR still exists for a real reason — and you might encounter it in enterprise environments.

beats.content: Use WAR when deploying to an existing application server that your operations team manages. Banks, government agencies, and large enterprises often have Tomcat clusters or JBoss/WebLogic deployments that predate the microservices era. Their deployment pipelines expect WARs.

beats.label: Three changes to make a Spring Boot WAR:
items: Set packaging to war in pom.xml
Mark spring-boot-starter-tomcat as provided scope (external server provides it)
Extend SpringBootServletInitializer in your main class

beats.content: non-obvious: Spring Boot WAR files are dual-mode. You can deploy the WAR to an external Tomcat AND run it with java -jar. Spring Boot detects the context and handles both startup paths. This is great during a migration from WAR to JAR — the same artifact works both ways.

sections.cap: Default to JAR for new projects. Choose WAR only when enterprise infrastructure demands it. If you must do WAR, Spring Boot's dual-mode support means you don't lose the ability to run it standalone.
